Name Above Every Name
NAYM uh-BUV EV-ree NAYM
n. (divine title phrase)
A phrase drawn directly from the MOOP translation of Philippians 2:9: “God highly exalted Him, and bestowed on Him the name that is above every name.” The Greek underlying “bestowed” is echarisato (graced, gifted) and “the name above every name” is to onoma to hyper pan onoma — an absolute superlative construction with no exceptions: above every name that can be named, in heaven or on earth.

Biblical Definition

The name above every name is the exalted designation bestowed upon the Lord Jesus Christ following His humiliation and atoning death — the name at which every knee in the entire created order will bow and every tongue will confess His lordship. Philippians 2:9–11 records the Christological hymn that grounds the title: “For this reason God highly exalted Him, and bestowed on Him the name that is above every name — so that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow — of those in heaven, and on earth, and under the earth.” The “name” in view is not merely a personal name but the authority, reputation, and recognized standing that the name encodes. In biblical thought a name is the bearer's identity, character, and right to be addressed — and Christ's name exceeds every name that could be given to any creature, any angel, any emperor, or any rival claimant. The exaltation is consequential: it follows upon the emptying and the obedience of the cross (Phil 2:7–8), making the name above every name the fruit of substitutionary humiliation. Paul's use in Acts 4:12 sharpens the soteriological edge: “There is no other name under heaven that has been given among men by which we must be saved.” The name is not merely incomparable in rank; it is exclusive in salvific efficacy. And Revelation 19:12 reveals that Christ has “a name written that no one knows except Himself” — suggesting that even the full weight of the name above every name exceeds creaturely comprehension and will be disclosed only in the consummation.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines name as the word by which a person or thing is called and known, and the reputation, character, and authority the name carries; the name above every name is therefore Christ's exalted standing and authority — surpassing every rank and title in the created and angelic orders.

expand to see more

NAME, n. The word or combination of words by which a person or thing is called and known; by extension, the reputation, authority, and recognized character of the bearer. Webster (1828) notes that to do something “in the name of” someone is to act by their authority and on their behalf.

The biblical category of “name” is thicker than mere nomenclature: a name in Scripture discloses character, authority, and covenantal standing. The name above every name is therefore the total exaltation of Christ — His authority over every power, His title to every worship, His right to the obedience of every creature who bears a name.

Key Scripture

Philippians 2:9 — "For this reason God highly exalted Him, and bestowed on Him the name that is above every name —"

Philippians 2:10 — "so that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow — of those in heaven, and on earth, and under the earth —"

Acts 4:12 — "And there is salvation in no one else — for there is no other name under heaven that has been given among men by which we must be saved."

John 8:58 — "Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you — before Abraham was, I AM.”"

Modern Corruption

Religious pluralism treats the name of Jesus as one saving name among many; therapeutic Christianity reduces the name above every name to an emotional comfort-word rather than the exclusive authority and title before which all creation must bow; prosperity theology exploits the name as a power-word to manipulate God.

expand to see more

Religious pluralism — the view that sincere faith in any deity leads to the same ultimate salvation — is the direct inversion of Acts 4:12. On the pluralist account, there is no name above every name, only a pantheon of equally valid salvific options. The apostle's grammar is exclusive and absolute: “no other name under heaven,” “no other” being a double negative in Greek (ouk estin en allo oudeni) that tolerates no exceptions. The name above every name claims a monopoly on saving authority precisely because the One who bears it is the only mediator between God and man (1 Tim 2:5).

Within popular charismatic and prosperity circles, “the name of Jesus” functions as a verbal formula for commanding healing, rebuking demons, and extracting divine resources — a verbal key to a cosmic vending machine. This inverts the directionality of Phil 2:9–11: it is not our knees bowing in submission to the name, but our use of the name to bend circumstances to our preferences. The name above every name demands surrender, not exploitation. Those who bear it rightly are bondservants who kneel; those who exploit it are rebels who grab.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The concept of a name that carries rank, authority, and the right to universal obedience runs through the entire biblical canon from the naming of Adam to the investiture hymn of Philippians 2 — Christ's name above every name is the culmination of the biblical theology of the divine name.

expand to see more

Greek to onoma to hyper pan onoma — “the name above every name” (Phil 2:9); hyper with accusative expressing surpassing superiority without qualification.

Hebrew shēm — name; in Old Testament theology a person's name encodes their character, authority, and standing before God and before the community.

Septuagint LXX — Greek rendering of the Hebrew divine name YHWH as Kyrios (Lord); when Phil 2:10 applies “Lord” to Jesus, it assigns the Septuagintal YHWH title to Him.

Phil 2:6–11 (Carmen Christi) — the Christological hymn that frames the exaltation: the name above every name is the crown given to the One who took “the form of a servant” and became “obedient to the point of death.”

Revelation 19:12 — Christ has “a name written that no one knows except Himself,” signalling that the full content of the name above every name exceeds creaturely knowing and awaits eschatological disclosure.

Usage

"The exaltation of the name above every name is the direct consequence of the cross: because Christ humbled Himself to death, the Father highly exalted Him — making the name the trophy of the atoning obedience, not a title seized by power."

"To pray “in the name of Jesus” is not to employ a verbal formula but to align one's petition with the authority, character, and purposes of the One who holds the name above every name — asking according to His will, not using His name to override it."

"Acts 4:12 uses the salvific exclusivity of the name as the ground for Peter's boldness before the Sanhedrin: the men who crucified Christ have no other name by which to be saved, and Peter will not supply one."
